notes:
1. Monetary Policy — Meaning and Authority

  • Monetary policy is the policy through which the Reserve Bank of India influences interest rates, liquidity, money and credit conditions in the economy.
  • It is one of the major instruments of macroeconomic management.
  • RBI formulates and implements monetary policy in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monetary Policy → RBI

2. Primary Objective — Price Stability with Growth in Mind

  • The primary statutory objective of monetary policy is to maintain price stability.
  • While maintaining price stability, RBI keeps the objective of economic growth in mind.
  • Stable prices protect purchasing power and improve predictability for households and businesses.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monetary Policy → Price Stability + Growth in Mind

3. Major Economic Effects

Monetary policy can influence:

  • Borrowing.
  • Lending.
  • Saving.
  • Investment.
  • Consumption.
  • Inflation.
  • Liquidity.
  • Credit conditions.
  • Economic activity.

4. Monetary Policy vs Fiscal Policy

Monetary policy:

  • RBI.
  • Interest rates.
  • Liquidity.
  • Money.
  • Credit.

Fiscal policy:

  • Government.
  • Taxation.
  • Expenditure.
  • Borrowing.
  • Budget.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monetary → RBI

Fiscal → Government

5. Evolution of India's Monetary Framework

Earlier RBI approaches included:

  • Credit controls.
  • Interest-rate regulation.
  • Reserve requirements.
  • Monetary targeting.
  • Multiple-indicator approaches.
  • Economic and financial reforms gradually made monetary policy more market-oriented.

6. Monetary Policy Framework Agreement — 2015

  • Government of India and RBI signed the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement in February 2015.
  • It strengthened the shift towards an explicit inflation-targeting framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monetary Policy Framework Agreement → February 2015

7. RBI Act Amendment — 2016

  • The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 was amended in 2016.
  • The amendment provided statutory backing to the modern monetary-policy framework.
  • It also gave statutory backing to the Monetary Policy Committee.
📌 Must-Memorise

2016 → Statutory Monetary Framework + MPC

8. Flexible Inflation Targeting — FIT

  • India adopted a Flexible Inflation Targeting framework.
  • FIT gives primary importance to keeping inflation around a prescribed target.
  • It does not require RBI to ignore growth, financial conditions or other macroeconomic risks.
📌 Must-Memorise

FIT → Flexible Inflation Targeting

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Flexible Inflation Targeting ≠ Inflation Only

9. Why Monetary Policy Is Forward-Looking

  • Monetary policy decisions affect the economy with a time lag.
  • RBI therefore examines expected inflation and future economic conditions, not merely current inflation.

Important factors include:

  • Inflation.
  • Growth.
  • Demand.
  • Financial conditions.
  • Global developments.
  • Commodity prices.
  • Other macroeconomic risks.

10. Operational Framework — Repo Rate and Liquidity

The modern framework broadly operates through:

  • Setting the policy repo rate.
  • Managing banking-system liquidity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monetary Framework → Repo Rate + Liquidity Management

11. CPI — Inflation Target Indicator

  • India's formal inflation-targeting framework uses Consumer Price Index inflation.
  • It does not use WPI as the formal target indicator.
📌 Must-Memorise

Inflation Target → CPI

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CPI → Yes

WPI → No

12. Inflation Target and Tolerance Band

According to the supplied material for the period 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031:

  • CPI inflation target → 4%.
  • Lower tolerance limit → 2%.
  • Upper tolerance limit → 6%.
📌 Must-Memorise

2% → 4% → 6%

13. Inflation Target — Important Interpretation

  • The framework does not require CPI inflation to remain exactly at 4% every month.
  • Inflation can temporarily fluctuate because of food prices, fuel prices, weather, commodity prices and supply shocks.
  • The objective is to keep inflation broadly around the prescribed target over the medium term.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

4% Target ≠ Inflation Must Always Equal 4%

14. Inflation-Target Accountability

  • Persistent inflation outside the statutory tolerance range can trigger accountability provisions under the RBI Act.
  • The framework therefore promotes greater transparency and accountability in monetary policymaking.

15. Monetary Policy Committee — MPC

  • MPC stands for Monetary Policy Committee.
  • It determines the policy repo rate.
  • Section 45ZB of the RBI Act provides for the MPC.
📌 Must-Memorise

MPC → Monetary Policy Committee

Section 45ZB → MPC

16. MPC — Six-Member Composition

The MPC has six members:

RBI side:

  • RBI Governor.
  • Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy.
  • One RBI officer nominated by the Central Board.

External side:

  • Three members appointed by the Central Government.
📌 Must-Memorise

MPC → 6 Members = 3 RBI + 3 External

17. MPC Chairperson and Voting

  • RBI Governor serves as Chairperson of the MPC.
  • Each member has one vote.
  • Policy decisions are taken according to the statutory voting procedure.
  • RBI publishes the MPC resolution after the meeting.
📌 Must-Memorise

MPC Chairperson → RBI Governor

18. MPC Minutes

  • Minutes of MPC meetings are published on the fourteenth day after the meeting under the statutory framework.
  • Published minutes include the vote and statement of each member.
📌 Must-Memorise

MPC Minutes → 14th Day

19. MPC — Core Identity

MPC =

6 Members

  • RBI Governor as Chairperson
  • Repo Rate Decision
  • Statutory Framework

20. Repo Rate — Meaning

  • Repo rate is the central policy interest rate in India's monetary-policy framework.
  • It is associated with short-term liquidity provided by RBI against eligible securities under a repurchase arrangement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Main Policy Rate → Repo Rate

21. Repo Rate Increase — Transmission Logic

When repo rate rises:

  • RBI borrowing cost for banks increases.
  • Bank lending rates may rise.
  • Loan demand may moderate.
  • Investment may slow.
  • Credit-financed consumption may decline.
  • Aggregate demand may weaken.
  • Inflationary pressure may reduce over time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Repo ↑ → Borrowing Cost ↑ → Demand ↓ → Inflation Pressure ↓

22. Repo Rate Reduction — Transmission Logic

When repo rate falls:

  • Borrowing conditions may become easier.
  • Lending rates may fall if transmission occurs.
  • Investment can increase.
  • Housing and other credit-financed consumption can strengthen.
  • Economic activity may receive support.
📌 Must-Memorise

Repo ↓ → Borrowing Cost ↓ → Demand ↑ → Growth Support

23. Repo Transmission Is Not Automatic

  • Repo-rate changes do not produce identical or immediate changes in every bank lending or deposit rate.
  • Transmission depends on bank funding costs, liquidity, credit risk, competition and financial-market conditions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Repo Change ≠ Instant Same Change in Every Loan Rate

24. Liquidity Adjustment Facility — LAF

  • LAF stands for Liquidity Adjustment Facility.
  • It forms part of RBI's framework for managing short-term liquidity and guiding money-market rates.
📌 Must-Memorise

LAF → Liquidity Adjustment Facility

25. Policy Corridor — SDF, Repo and MSF

The present operating corridor is represented as:

SDF → Repo Rate → MSF

  • SDF forms the lower side.
  • Repo is the central policy rate.
  • MSF forms the upper side.
📌 Must-Memorise

SDF → Floor

Repo → Centre

MSF → Ceiling

26. Standing Deposit Facility — SDF

  • SDF stands for Standing Deposit Facility.
  • It allows eligible banks to place surplus funds with RBI.
  • It therefore absorbs liquidity.
  • SDF was introduced in 2022.
  • It forms the floor of the present policy corridor.
📌 Must-Memorise

SDF → Absorbs Liquidity + Corridor Floor + 2022

27. SDF — Collateral Feature

  • Unlike traditional reverse-repo transactions, SDF does not require RBI to provide collateral for liquidity absorption.

28. Marginal Standing Facility — MSF

  • MSF stands for Marginal Standing Facility.
  • It provides overnight liquidity to eligible banks under specified conditions.
  • Banks may use it to manage unexpected short-term liquidity shortages.
  • MSF normally forms the ceiling of the policy corridor.
📌 Must-Memorise

MSF → Overnight Liquidity + Corridor Ceiling

29. Bank Rate

  • Bank Rate is a rate specified by RBI under its statutory framework.
  • In the operating arrangement described in the supplied material, Bank Rate is aligned with the MSF rate.

30. Reverse Repo — Historical Corridor Role

  • Fixed reverse repo previously served as an important lower-side facility in the LAF corridor.
  • After introduction of SDF in 2022, SDF became the operative standing facility forming the corridor floor.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Current Corridor Floor → SDF

Not Fixed Reverse Repo

31. Cash Reserve Ratio — CRR

  • CRR stands for Cash Reserve Ratio.
  • Specified banks maintain a prescribed proportion of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities as cash balances with RBI.
📌 Must-Memorise

CRR → Cash with RBI

32. NDTL — Net Demand and Time Liabilities

  • NDTL stands for Net Demand and Time Liabilities.
  • Both CRR and SLR are commonly expressed with reference to NDTL.
📌 Must-Memorise

NDTL → Net Demand and Time Liabilities

33. CRR — Liquidity Effect

CRR increase:

  • More funds remain with RBI.
  • Lendable resources with banks decline.

CRR decrease:

  • More funds are released to banks.
  • Lendable resources increase.
📌 Must-Memorise

CRR ↑ → Liquidity ↓

CRR ↓ → Liquidity ↑

34. Statutory Liquidity Ratio — SLR

  • SLR stands for Statutory Liquidity Ratio.
  • Banks maintain a prescribed proportion of NDTL in eligible liquid assets.
  • Eligible assets can include specified liquid assets and government securities.
  • SLR is primarily associated with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
📌 Must-Memorise

SLR → Statutory Liquidity Ratio

SLR → Banking Regulation Act, 1949

35. CRR vs SLR

CRR:

  • Cash balance.
  • Maintained with RBI.

SLR:

  • Eligible liquid assets.
  • Maintained by banks themselves.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CRR ≠ SLR

36. Open Market Operations — OMO

  • OMO stands for Open Market Operations.
  • RBI buys or sells government securities in the market to influence liquidity.
📌 Must-Memorise

OMO → RBI Purchase / Sale of Government Securities

37. OMO — Liquidity Effect

OMO purchase:

  • RBI buys securities.
  • Liquidity generally enters the financial system.

OMO sale:

  • RBI sells securities.
  • Liquidity generally moves out of the financial system.
📌 Must-Memorise

OMO Buy → Liquidity ↑

OMO Sell → Liquidity ↓

38. OMO — Durable Liquidity

  • OMO can influence more durable liquidity conditions rather than only overnight liquidity.

39. Banking-System Liquidity

  • Liquidity means availability of short-term funds in the financial system.

Liquidity surplus:

  • Banks collectively have excess short-term funds.

Liquidity deficit:

  • Banks collectively require additional short-term funds.

40. Major Liquidity Instruments

RBI can manage liquidity through:

  • Repo operations.
  • SDF.
  • MSF.
  • OMO.
  • Variable-rate operations.

41. Variable Rate Repo — VRR

  • VRR stands for Variable Rate Repo.
  • VRR auctions can inject liquidity at rates determined through the auction process.
📌 Must-Memorise

VRR → Injects Liquidity

42. Variable Rate Reverse Repo — VRRR

  • VRRR stands for Variable Rate Reverse Repo.
  • It can absorb surplus liquidity through an auction-based mechanism.
📌 Must-Memorise

VRRR → Absorbs Liquidity

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

VRR ≠ VRRR

43. Why Liquidity Management Matters

  • Repo-rate changes are less effective if short-term market rates do not move consistently with the monetary-policy stance.
  • Liquidity management therefore helps monetary-policy transmission.

44. Money Supply — Meaning

  • Money supply refers to the stock of money available in the economy at a particular time.
  • Different monetary aggregates measure different degrees of money and liquidity.

45. Reserve Money — High-Powered Money

  • Reserve money is also called high-powered money.
  • It broadly includes currency in circulation and specified deposits with RBI.
  • It forms the monetary base of the economy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Reserve Money → High-Powered Money

46. Narrow Money and Broad Money

Narrow money:

  • Highly liquid forms of money readily usable for transactions.

Broad money:

  • Narrow money plus a wider range of bank deposits.

47. M3 — Broad Money

  • In India, M3 is commonly used as an important measure of broad money.
📌 Must-Memorise

M3 → Broad Money

48. Factors Affecting Money Supply

Money supply is influenced by:

  • Currency demand.
  • Bank deposits.
  • Bank credit.
  • RBI operations.
  • Government transactions.
  • Capital flows.

49. Modern Monetary Policy — Interest-Rate Framework

  • Modern RBI policy does not mechanically target a fixed quantity of money.
  • The policy repo rate and liquidity management form the main operating framework.
  • Monetary and financial aggregates are nevertheless monitored.

50. Expansionary Monetary Policy

Expansionary policy seeks easier monetary and credit conditions.

It can involve:

  • Lower policy rates.
  • Greater liquidity.
  • Lower borrowing costs.
  • Higher credit demand.
  • More investment.
  • More consumption.
📌 Must-Memorise

Expansionary Monetary Policy → Easier Credit Conditions

51. When Expansionary Policy Is Used

  • It is generally more suitable when economic growth is weak and inflationary pressure is manageable.
  • Its purpose is to support demand, investment and economic activity.

52. Contractionary Monetary Policy

Contractionary policy seeks tighter monetary and credit conditions.

It can involve:

  • Higher policy rates.
  • Tighter liquidity.
  • Higher borrowing costs.
  • Lower loan demand.
  • Moderation of consumption.
  • Moderation of investment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Contractionary Monetary Policy → Tighter Credit Conditions

53. Contractionary Policy — Inflation Effect

  • Lower aggregate demand can reduce inflationary pressure over time.
  • However, excessive tightening can weaken growth and employment.

54. Expansionary vs Contractionary Policy

  • Expansionary → Easier money + demand support.
  • Contractionary → Tighter money + demand restraint.

55. Monetary Policy Transmission — Meaning

  • Monetary-policy transmission is the process through which RBI policy decisions affect financial markets, bank rates and the wider economy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Policy Decision → Market Rates → Bank Rates → Demand → Output → Inflation

56. Interest-Rate Channel

  • Policy-rate changes influence short-term market rates and bank funding costs.
  • These can influence lending and deposit rates.
  • Changes in lending rates affect household and business borrowing.
  • Deposit-rate changes can influence saving behaviour.

57. Credit Channel

  • Tighter monetary conditions can make credit more expensive or less easily available.
  • Easier conditions can support bank lending.

58. Expectations Channel

  • Monetary-policy decisions influence expectations about future inflation and interest rates.
  • Stable inflation expectations can improve policy effectiveness.

59. Exchange-Rate Channel

  • Interest rates and liquidity conditions can influence capital flows and foreign-exchange-market conditions.
  • Exchange-rate changes can affect import prices and inflation.
  • Exchange rates also depend on many other domestic and global factors.

60. Asset-Price Channel

  • Interest-rate changes can influence bond yields, equity valuations, property demand and other asset prices.
  • Changes in asset values can affect investment, wealth and spending decisions.

61. Why Transmission Can Be Weak

Transmission may be affected by:

  • Bank deposit costs.
  • Banking-system liquidity.
  • Weak bank balance sheets.
  • Borrower creditworthiness.
  • Competition among banks.
  • Bond-market conditions.
  • Sticky or administered interest rates.

62. Basis Points — Interest-Rate Measurement

  • A basis point is used to express small changes in interest rates.
📌 Must-Memorise

100 basis points = 1 percentage point

50 basis points = 0.50 percentage point

25 basis points = 0.25 percentage point

63. Repo Change vs Loan Rate Change

  • A 25-basis-point repo change does not automatically produce a 25-basis-point change in every lending rate.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

25 bp Repo Change ≠ Automatic 25 bp Loan-Rate Change

64. Inflation-Growth Trade-Off

  • Persistent high inflation may require tighter monetary conditions.
  • Very high interest rates can weaken investment, consumption and growth.
  • If growth is weak and inflation permits, monetary easing can support economic activity.

65. Supply-Side Inflation — Monetary Policy Limitation

  • Monetary policy is less effective when inflation is caused mainly by supply shortages.
  • Higher interest rates cannot directly produce more food during crop failure.
  • Monetary policy cannot directly increase global crude-oil supply.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Repo Rate ↑ Cannot Directly Produce More Food or Oil

66. Supply Shocks and Second-Round Inflation

  • RBI can still act to prevent temporary supply shocks from becoming broad and persistent inflation.
  • Monetary policy can also help prevent temporary price shocks from becoming embedded in inflation expectations.

67. Headline Inflation

  • Headline inflation measures overall inflation in the consumer basket.
  • It includes food and fuel.
📌 Must-Memorise

Headline Inflation → Includes Food + Fuel

68. Core Inflation

  • Core inflation generally attempts to measure underlying inflation after excluding volatile food and fuel components.
📌 Must-Memorise

Core Inflation → Commonly Excludes Food + Fuel

69. Formal Inflation Target — Headline CPI

  • India's formal inflation target is based on headline CPI inflation.
  • Core inflation is an analytical measure, not the sole formal target.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Formal Target → Headline CPI

Not Core Inflation Alone

70. Monetary and Fiscal Policy — Interaction

During inflation:

  • Monetary policy may raise interest rates.
  • Fiscal policy may restrain expenditure or increase taxation.

During slowdown:

  • Monetary policy may ease financing conditions.
  • Fiscal policy may directly increase government spending.

71. Policy Coordination

  • Monetary and fiscal policies can reinforce or offset each other.
  • If fiscal policy is highly expansionary while monetary policy is tightening, the two can partly work in opposite directions.
  • Coordination may become especially important during severe economic shocks.

72. Monetary Policy — Time Lag

  • Monetary policy does not affect inflation and growth immediately.
  • Changes pass through markets, banks, borrowers and spending decisions over time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monetary Policy → Works with Time Lag

73. Major Challenges to Monetary Policy

Important challenges include:

  • Weak transmission.
  • Informal finance.
  • Global interest-rate changes.
  • Foreign-capital flows.
  • Oil-price changes.
  • Geopolitical events.
  • Growth-inflation trade-offs.
  • Financial-stability risks.

74. Informal Finance — Transmission Limitation

  • Sections of the economy dependent on informal credit may respond less directly to RBI policy-rate changes.

75. Global Factors

Monetary conditions can be affected by:

  • International interest rates.
  • Sudden capital inflows.
  • Sudden capital outflows.
  • Global commodity prices.
  • Crude-oil prices.
  • Wars and geopolitical disruptions.

76. Financial-Stability Trade-Off

  • Very low interest rates maintained for long periods may encourage excessive borrowing or risk-taking.
  • Rapid monetary tightening can increase repayment stress for borrowers.
  • RBI therefore balances inflation, growth, liquidity, credit conditions and financial stability.

Inflation and Growth Assessment

→ MPC Decision

→ Repo Rate + Liquidity Management

→ Financial-Market Transmission

→ Demand, Output and Inflation

This is the central policy chain.

92. TNPSC Traps

  • Monetary policy is primarily associated with RBI.
  • Fiscal policy is primarily associated with Government.
  • Primary objective is price stability while keeping growth in mind.
  • India follows Flexible Inflation Targeting.
  • Monetary Policy Framework Agreement → 2015.
  • RBI Act amendment for modern MPC framework → 2016.
  • Inflation targeting uses CPI, not WPI.
  • Target stated in the supplied period → 4%.
  • Tolerance band → 2% to 6%.
  • Inflation need not equal exactly 4% every month.
  • MPC has six members.
  • MPC has three RBI-side and three external members.
  • RBI Governor chairs MPC.
  • MPC determines the policy repo rate.
  • Section 45ZB → MPC.
  • Repo rate is not a rate at which ordinary citizens directly borrow from RBI.
  • Repo increase is generally contractionary.
  • Repo reduction is generally expansionary.
  • SDF absorbs liquidity.
  • SDF is the corridor floor.
  • SDF was introduced in 2022.
  • MSF provides overnight liquidity.
  • MSF is the corridor ceiling.
  • Fixed reverse repo should not be treated as the operative corridor floor after SDF introduction.
  • CRR is cash maintained with RBI.
  • SLR is maintained by banks in eligible liquid assets.
  • CRR and SLR are different.
  • CRR increase generally reduces lendable funds.
  • CRR reduction generally releases liquidity.
  • OMO purchase injects liquidity.
  • OMO sale absorbs liquidity.
  • VRR injects liquidity.
  • VRRR absorbs liquidity.
  • Reserve money = high-powered money.
  • M3 = broad money.
  • 100 basis points = 1 percentage point.
  • 25 basis points = 0.25 percentage point.
  • Repo changes are not transmitted instantly or equally to every lending rate.
  • Headline inflation includes food and fuel.
  • Core inflation commonly excludes food and fuel.
  • Formal inflation targeting uses headline CPI.
  • Monetary policy cannot directly solve crop failure or crude-oil shortage.
  • Monetary policy works with a time lag.
  • Current rates can change.
  • Economic projections are forecasts, not guaranteed outcomes.

  • 100 basis points? → 1 percentage point.

  • Can monetary policy directly solve crop failure? → No.
